{{short description|On structure of ω-bounded connected surfaces}}
{{Only primary sources|date=January 2022}}
[[File:Chambers 1908 Bagpipe.png|thumb|right]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''bagpipe theorem''' of Peter Nyikos describes the structure of the connected (but possibly non-[[paracompact space|paracompact]]) [[ω-bounded space|ω-bounded]] surfaces by showing that they are "bagpipes": the [[connected sum]] of a [[compact space|compact]] "bag" with several "long pipes".<ref name="Nyikos1984"> {{Cite book |last=Nyikos |first=Peter |title=Handbook of Set-Theoretic Topology |publisher=North Holland |year=1984 |isbn=978-0-444-86580-9 |editor-last=Kunen |editor-first=Kenneth |editor-link=Kenneth Kunen |pages=633–684 |chapter=The theory of nonmetrizable manifolds |doi=10.1016/B978-0-444-86580-9.50017-3 |mr=0776633 |editor-last2=Vaughan |editor-first2=Jerry E.}}
</ref>

==Statement==
A space is called [[ω-bounded]] if the closure of every countable set is compact. Compactness implies ω-boundedness, but in general the converse is not true. For example, the [[first uncountable ordinal]] <math>\omega_1</math> with the order topology and the [[long line (topology)|long line]] are both ω-bounded but not compact. For metric spaces, however, the two concepts are equivalent.

The bagpipe theorem states that every ω-bounded connected surface is the connected sum of a compact connected surface and a finite number of ''long pipes'' (defined below).  

A space P is called a long pipe if there exist subspaces <math>\{U_\alpha: \alpha < \omega_1 \} </math> each of which is homeomorphic to <math>S^1 \times \mathbb{R} </math> such that for <math>n<m</math>, <math> \overline{U_n} \subseteq U_m</math> and the boundary of <math>U_n</math> in <math>U_m</math> is homeomorphic to <math>S^1</math>. The simplest example of a long pipe is the product <math>S^1 \times L^+</math> of the circle <math>S^1</math> and the long closed ray <math>L^+</math>, which is an increasing union of <math>\omega_1</math> copies of the half-open interval <math>[0,1)</math>, pasted together with the lexicographic ordering. Another long pipe is obtained by removing a single point from the "long plane" <math>L \times L</math>, where <math>L</math> is the long line. There are in fact <math>2^{\aleph_1}</math> different isomorphism classes of long pipes. 

The bagpipe theorem does not describe all surfaces since there are many examples of surfaces that are not ω-bounded, such as the [[Prüfer manifold]].
